title: Eid around the world
hookLine: Lebaran in Indonesia, Bayram in Turkey, Sallah in Nigeria

cards: The month of fasting is over. In Jakarta, the roads out of the city jam for days beforehand, as families crowd onto trains, buses and ferries, heading back to the villages they came from.
In Istanbul, children make the rounds of relatives, kissing their elders' hands and pressing them to their foreheads, and coming away with sweets.
In northern Nigeria, horsemen in bright robes and turbans ride in procession before the emir, drums going, crowds cheering. Three countries, three languages. One festival.

teach.b: First, the two days. A hadith recorded by Abu Dawud tells that when the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, came to Medina, the people there had two days a year for games and play.
He told them God had given them two better days instead: the day of sacrifice, Eid al-Adha, and the day of breaking the fast, Eid al-Fitr. Today is mostly the second, the Eid that ends Ramadan.
The Qur'an, speaking of the fast, says it is so that, in Pickthall's words, "ye should magnify Allah for having guided you, and that peradventure ye may be thankful."
The festival is gratitude out loud: the takbir sung on the way to prayer, God is greater, over and over. Third, the names.
In Indonesia, Eid is Lebaran, a season for going home and asking forgiveness: people say a phrase asking pardon for any wrong, outward or inward.
In Turkey it's Bayram, and Ramazan Bayramı is also called Şeker Bayramı, the sugar holiday, for the sweets.
In Nigeria, in Hausa, it's Sallah, and in some northern cities the celebration includes a durbar, a grand procession of horsemen. Fourth, what's the same.
Before the Eid prayer, a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari says, a small charity is given, a measure of dates or barley: zakat al-fitr. Then prayer together in the morning, best clothes, visits, food.
And one greeting is heard in many countries: Eid Mubarak. A blessed Eid.

how: Muslims mark Eid al-Fitr at the end of Ramadan with charity for the poor before the prayer, a congregational prayer in the morning, new or best clothes, family visits and the greeting Eid Mubarak.

practice: Say it once, quietly: Eid Mubarak, blessed Eid. Then picture someone you might say it to next Eid, a neighbor, a coworker, a shopkeeper you see every week, and their face when they hear it.
If you're Muslim, think of someone in your family you'd like to visit, or to ask forgiveness from, as people do at Lebaran in Indonesia; if you pray, give thanks for being guided.

wordCard.voice: Eid Mubarak, the greeting heard in many languages and countries when the fast ends and the festival begins. Today's word.
